A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same theoretical framework and numerical experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–F are readable and support comparison, including matching the reordered theory appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original transformer experiments on linear regression, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, and Volterra processes in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck analysis across finite numbers of pretraining tasks in Appendix B.2.

M1.justification: The transformer architectures, next-sample prediction objectives, and importance-reweighting procedure are retained. Appendix B.4 explains previously used reweighting; the repeated-task extension concerns theoretical analysis rather than a newly implemented learning method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three numerical task families, prior families, and task-shift scenarios. The additional OU experiment varies training-task counts within existing coverage. Natural-language and tabular applications remain discussion rather than new evaluations.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Ridge regression for linear regression and ARMA and last-value predictors for OU and Volterra processes. v2 Table 1 compares theoretical coverage of prior work; it does not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 Figure 13 adds OU evaluations with 100, 500, and 1000 pretraining tasks. Section 4 also replaces the description of evaluation tasks as shifted draws from each training prior with a common shifted Gaussian. This corrects the main-text description to match v1 Appendix C.1; it does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B.2 adds an OU task-count sensitivity analysis testing the generalization cost of heavier-tailed priors. Existing linear-regression variance and task-count analyses, Volterra dependence analyses, context-length comparisons, and reweighting experiments are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three repetitions with different seeds in Appendix C.2. Shaded uncertainty bands already appear in v1, and v2 introduces no documented change to uncertainty estimation, run counts, or significance testing.

E6.justification: v2 Figure 13 adds OU best, mean, and full-context MSE results for 100, 500, and 1000 pretraining tasks, supporting the finite-data qualification of heavy-tail benefits. Existing experimental graphics retain their results despite relocation and rearrangement; the addition does not demonstrate improved performance under an unchanged setting.

T1.justification: The two central theorem bounds are retained and reordered, but v2 adds distribution-shift risk transfer in D.6, repeated-task bounds and proof sketches in D.7, finite-prior analysis in Remark E.1, and a Rényi-to-prediction-error derivation in F.2. It also substantively repairs the conditional norm-sub-Gaussian assumption and supporting lemma, including changed constants, and corrects task-selection proof equations.

C1.justification: The framework, heavy-tail/dependence guarantees, numerical validation, and trade-off between robust task selection and generalization were already claimed in v1, including Section 3.3 and the conclusion. v2 foregrounds that trade-off in its title, abstract, and contribution list without changing the central scientific claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation connecting generalization to the in-weight/in-context learning transition, practical implications for tabular and text pretraining, and possible inference-cost benefits. Its new limitations section explicitly discusses conditional sub-Gaussianity, the Bayesian-optimality gap, and the indirect nature of prediction-error evidence for task selection, substantially extending v1's primarily numerical-scope limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 gives more explicit instructions for constructing uniform-target importance weights. Conversely, Appendix C removes the implementation-source repository link and code-provenance statement present in v1. Data generation, architectures, optimization settings, training budgets, and hardware disclosures otherwise remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises positioning, identifies Zhang et al. (2025b) as the closest framework, and adds a structured comparison table. New discussion engages learning-transition work by Park, Wurgaft, and Nguyen and Reddy, alongside additional numerical, attention-regularity, and tabular-foundation-model references. Appendix A is largely retained.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, theoretical explanations, experimental narrative, and conclusion. It reverses the generalization/task-selection order and corresponding appendices, adds a theoretical-predictions summary and discussion section, and consolidates reweighting discussion in Appendix B.4.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two columns. Existing plots are cropped, regrouped, and redistributed between the main text and appendix; the distribution-parameter table moves to Appendix B. v2 also adds the research-positioning table and OU task-count figure. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 clarifies the existing trade-off, repairs the formal conditional norm-sub-Gaussian assumption and lemma, adds useful OU evidence, and states important limitations more precisely. These support a modest net improvement. However, the new Appendix F.2 contains an incorrect Gaussian-integral coefficient between F.21 and F.22, weakening its claimed Rényi-to-MSE connection, and Appendix C removes the implementation-source link. The expanded theory therefore does not warrant an unqualified assessment of substantial improvement.
